extracted.intended_audience: federal judges and patent litigators drafting or using jury instructions (and jurors receiving those instructions)
extracted.subtask_description: Model AIPLA jury instructions on patent infringement and invalidity issues under U.S. law, covering elements and burdens for §271(g) infringement, definitions of prior art (pre-AIA and AIA), anticipation, public use, on-sale bar, experimental use, printed publications, prior invention/patents, and related evidentiary guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement under 35 U.S.C. § 271(g)
rubrics_metrics.description: [the Defendant] [[imported into the United States or,] within the United States, [sold] [offered for sale] [used]] a product that was made by a process that includes all steps of at least one claim of the [abbreviated patent number] patent; the product was made between [issue date of patent] and [[expiration date of patent] [date of trial]]; and [the Defendant] [[imported into the United States or,] within the United States, [sold] [offered for sale] [used]] the product between [issue date of patent] and [[expiration date of patent] [date of trial]].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You must decide whether the evidence establishes that the product [[imported] [sold] [offered for sale] [used]] by the Defendant was “made by” the claimed process. If the product was materially changed by later processes, or the product is only a trivial or non-essential part of another product, then it was not “made by” the claimed process. Infringement under Section 271(g) does not require that a single entity perform the patented process. (Cites: 35 U.S.C. § 271(g); cases including Syngenta, Amgen, Microsoft v. AT&T, WesternGeco.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of Proof for Invalidity (clear and convincing)
rubrics_metrics.description: [The Defendant] must prove by clear and convincing evidence that each asserted claim is invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims of an issued patent may be found invalid, but the defendant bears the heightened burden of clear and convincing evidence for each asserted claim. This burden never changes regardless of whether the Patent Examiner considered the reference. (Cites: Microsoft v. i4i and related guidance.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior Art Defined (pre-AIA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art includes items received into evidence during trial such as: any [[product] [method]] that was publicly known or used by others in the United States before the claimed invention was invented; any [[product] [method]] that was in public use or on sale in the United States before [Cutoff Date]; any patents that issued before [Cutoff Date]; any publications having dates of public accessibility before [Cutoff Date]; and any [[product] [method]] that was made by anyone in the United States before the date of invention where the claimed invention was not later abandoned, suppressed, or concealed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify the prior art items admitted into evidence. If parties dispute status of a reference as prior art due to date, public availability, or other factors, those issues should be identified to the jury. (Statutory cite: 35 U.S.C. § 102 (pre-AIA).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior Art Defined (AIA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art includes: anything that was patented, described in a printed publication, or in public use, on sale, or otherwise available to the public anywhere in the world before the effective filing date of claim(s) ___; and anything that was described in a patent, or in an application for patent published or deemed published, in which the patent or application names another inventor and was filed before the effective filing date of claim(s) ___.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify items contended as prior art. Use the effective filing date of the claims when determining AIA prior art. (Statutory cites: 35 U.S.C. § 102 as amended by the AIA; 35 U.S.C. § 100(i); Helsinn v. Teva.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions to Prior Art (AIA limited exceptions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A disclosure made one year or less before the effective filing date shall not be prior art if: A) the disclosure was made by the inventor or person who obtained the subject matter directly or indirectly from such inventor; or B) the subject matter disclosed had, before such disclosure, been publicly disclosed by the inventor or another who obtained the subject matter directly or indirectly from such inventor. Additional exceptions: disclosure obtained from inventor; subject matter and claimed invention owned by same person or subject to same obligation of assignment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If factual issues (e.g., whether public availability results from a disclosure within one year by inventor or derived from inventor, or ownership/assignment questions) exist, instruct the jury on these specific exceptions under § 102(b) and (c) as needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effect of Whether Prior Art Was Considered by the USPTO
rubrics_metrics.description: Regardless of whether a particular prior art reference was considered by the Patent Examiner during prosecution, the Defendant must prove invalidity by clear and convincing evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the PTO did not have all material facts before it, the PTO’s considered judgment may lose significant force. It may be appropriate to instruct the jury to evaluate whether the evidence is materially new compared to what the PTO considered, and to consider that fact when determining whether invalidity has been proven by clear and convincing evidence. (Cites: Microsoft v. i4i; Sciele Pharma v. Lupin.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Invalidity of Independent and Dependent Claims (claim-by-claim evaluation)
rubrics_metrics.description: An independent claim does not refer to any other claim; a dependent claim refers to at least one other claim and includes all elements recited in the dependent claim as well as all elements of the claim to which it refers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate invalidity on a claim-by-claim basis. If an independent claim is invalid, dependent claims are not automatically invalid. However, if a dependent claim is invalid, then the independent claim from which it depends must also be found invalid. (Cites: Comaper v. Antec; Callaway Golf; Ormco v. Align.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Person of Ordinary Skill in the Art (POSITA) Standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Invalidity of a patent claim is determined from the perspective of a person of ordinary skill in the art in the field of the claimed invention as of the [time of the invention/effective filing date].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this POSITA perspective when evaluating anticipation, obviousness, enablement, and what a prior reference would have conveyed to one of ordinary skill. (Cites: 35 U.S.C. § 103; KSR.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation (novelty) Standard
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove anticipation, the Defendant must prove that the claimed invention is not new by clear and convincing evidence. To anticipate a claim, each element in the claim must be present in a single item of prior art and arranged or combined in the same way as recited in the claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: You may not combine two or more items of prior art to find anticipation. In determining whether elements of the claimed invention are found in a prior reference, consider what a person of ordinary skill in the art would have understood from review of that reference. If elements are alleged to be inherent in a single prior art reference, instruct on inherency. (Cites: NetMoneyIN v. Verisign; Toro v. Deere; other Federal Circuit cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Inherency in Anticipation
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior art inherently anticipates a patent claim if the missing element(s) or feature(s) would necessarily result from what the single item of prior art teaches to a person of ordinary skill in the art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A party claiming inherent anticipation must prove that the allegedly inherent element(s) necessarily exist by clear and convincing evidence. Evidence outside the prior art reference (including experimental testing) may be used to show inherency. It is not required that persons of ordinary skill recognized or appreciated the inherent disclosure at the time the prior art was known. Likely presence is insufficient; necessity is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior Public Knowledge (pre-AIA)
rubrics_metrics.description: [The Defendant] contends that claim(s) ___ are invalid because the invention defined in that claim(s) was publicly known by others in the United States before [§ 102(a) (pre-AIA) Cutoff Date].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim is invalid if the invention was publicly known by others in the U.S. before it was invented by the patentee. If there is a factual issue regarding date of invention or priority date, instruct the jury on how to determine the Cutoff Date. (Cites: pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. § 102(a).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior Public Knowledge (AIA)
rubrics_metrics.description: [The Defendant] contends that claim(s) ___ are invalid because the claimed invention was available to the public before [§ 102(a) (AIA) Cutoff Date].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A claim is invalid if the claimed invention was available to the public before the effective filing date. If factual issues arise (e.g., disclosure within one year, derivation, or ownership issues), instruct the jury on exceptions under § 102(b) and (c) as needed. (Cites: 35 U.S.C. § 102(a)(1) (AIA).)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior Public Use (pre-AIA) — definition and readiness for patenting
rubrics_metrics.description: [The Defendant] contends that claim(s) ___ are invalid because the invention defined in that claim(s) was publicly used by others in the United States before [Cutoff Date]. An invention was publicly used in the U.S. if an embodiment was both: (1) accessible to the public or commercially exploited in the United States, and (2) ready for patenting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors relevant to determining public use include nature of the public activity, public access, confidentiality obligations, commercial exploitation, and circumstances of testing/experimentation. To be ready for patenting, the invention must be reduced to practice or the inventor must have prepared drawings/descriptions enabling a POSITA to make or use it. Reduction to practice requires constructing an embodiment or performing a process and determining that it works for its intended purpose. (Cites: pre-AIA 35 U.S.C. § 102(a),(b); Pfaff; cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior Public Use (AIA) — worldwide public use / commercial exploitation
rubrics_metrics.description: [The Defendant] contends that claim(s) ___ are invalid because the claimed invention was in public use anywhere in the world before [effective filing date]. An invention was in public use if the claimed invention was accessible to the public or commercially exploited anywhere in the world.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public use is use by the inventor or by a person not under secrecy obligations; absence of affirmative steps to conceal is evidence of public use. Commercial exploitation (e.g., selling a product made using an invention or promoting a product embodying an invention) can be public use even if specifics kept secret. To be a public use the invention also must have been ready for patenting (reduced to practice or enabling drawings). (Cites: 35 U.S.C. § 102(a)(1) (AIA).)

rubrics_metrics.name: On-Sale Bar
rubrics_metrics.description: [The Defendant] contends that claim ___ is invalid because the invention defined in that claim was on sale [[if pre-AIA:] in the United States] before [[Cutoff Date]]. That claim is invalid if before the Cutoff Date an embodiment of the claimed invention was both (1) the subject of a commercial sale or offer for sale [[if pre-AIA only:] in the United States], and (2) ready for patenting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A commercial offer for sale exists if another party could make a binding contract by simply accepting the offer. An invention embodied in an actual product was subject to an offer for sale if commercially sold or offered, even if done confidentially. It is not required that a sale occurred or that sale terms disclose invention details. The invention must have been ready for patenting at the time of sale/offer (reduced to practice or enabling drawings). (Cites: Pfaff; Helsinn; Medicines Co.; other cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental Use Exception
rubrics_metrics.description: [The Plaintiff] contends that ______________ should not be considered [[a prior public use] [placing the invention on sale]] because that [[use] [sale]] was experimental. Certain activities are experimental if they are a legitimate effort to test claimed features or to determine if the invention will work for its intended purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only experimentation by or under control of the inventor (or assignee) qualifies. Experimentation by third parties does not qualify. Experimental activity must relate to claimed features and be for technological improvement, not commercial exploitation; incidental profit is permitted. Tests primarily for marketing are not experimental. If defendant shows prior public use/sale by clear and convincing evidence, the burden shifts to plaintiff to produce evidence the purpose was experimental; if plaintiff's evidence is strong enough, jury may find no public use/sale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed Publication as Prior Art
rubrics_metrics.description: [The Defendant] contends that claim ___ is invalid because the invention was described in a printed publication before the Cutoff Date. A printed publication maintained in tangible form (e.g., printed pages, electronic file, microfilm, photographs, Internet publication) sufficiently accessible to persons interested can be prior art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accessibility: information is publicly accessible if persons interested and ordinarily skilled exercising reasonable diligence could locate it. It need not be available to every member of the public. An issued patent or a published patent application is a printed publication. The disclosure must be enabling—complete enough to enable a POSITA to use the invention without undue experimentation, considering what a POSITA would have known as of the Cutoff Date. (Cites: 35 U.S.C. § 102(a)/(b) pre-AIA; §102(a)(1)/(2) AIA; case law.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior Invention (pre-AIA only)
rubrics_metrics.description: [The Defendant] contends that claim ___ is invalid because the invention was invented by another person in the United States before the patentee. That claim is invalid if the prior person reduced to practice a product/method that included all features of the claim before the patentee, or was first to conceive and exercised reasonable diligence to reduce to practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defendant must show by clear and convincing evidence either (1) prior reduction to practice of all claim features, or (2) prior conception plus reasonable diligence until reduction to practice. The prior invention must be sufficiently developed that one skilled in the art would recognize it would work for its intended purpose. The defense may be negated if the prior invention was abandoned, suppressed, or concealed; jury may be instructed on evidence of abandonment/suppression/concealment. (Cites: 35 U.S.C. § 102(a),(g) pre-AIA; cases.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior Patent as Prior Art (pre-AIA)
rubrics_metrics.description: [The Defendant] contends that claim(s) ___ are invalid because the invention was disclosed in a patent by [third party] before the Cutoff Date. A patent disclosure in the United States or a foreign country before the Cutoff Date can render the claim invalid.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a factual issue exists regarding date of invention or priority, instruct the jury on how to determine invention date; otherwise instruct the jury as to the Cutoff Date. (Cites: 35 U.S.C. § 102(a),(b) pre-AIA; relevant Federal Circuit cases.)
